e-3624.worked_solution:
The derivative of $e^x$ is just $e^x$ itself. On the other hand, $\ln 3$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

Using the addition rule, then, we have 

$$
\eqalign{
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3e^x + \ln 3\right)\
                                                  &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( 3e^x\right) +  \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( \ln 3 \right)\
                                                  &= 3\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right) + 0\
                                                  &= 3 e^x.
}
$$

e-3625.knowledge_point: Differentiating the Product of a Constant and the Exponential Function, Plus a Polynomial
e-3625.worked_solution:
Using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\eqalign{ 
                          f'(x)             &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4e^x+3x^{4} - x^2 \right)\
                                             &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4e^x\right)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3x^{4}\right) -\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^{2}\right) \
					     &= 4\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right)+3\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^{4}\right) - 2x \			
                                             &=  4 e^x+  3 \cdot 4x^{3} - 2x \
                                             &=  4 e^x+  12x^{3} - 2x.
}
$$

e-3626.knowledge_point: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Base Other Than e
e-3626.worked_solution:
Applying the formula, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		f'(x)      &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3 \cdot 2^x\right) \
                            &= 3 \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(2^x\right) \
                            &=  3 \cdot 2^{x}\ln(2) \
                            &=  3 \ln(2) \cdot 2^{x}.
	}
$$

decision.explanation: The constant 10 has derivative 0, and the derivative of -2e^x is -2e^x. Thus f'(x)=-2e^x.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
The derivative of ${e}^{x}$ is just ${e}^{x}$ itself. On the other hand, $10$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

Using the addition rule, then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(10-2{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(10)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2{e}^{x}) \\  & =0-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x}) \\  & =-2{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

f′(x)=ddx(10−2ex)=ddx(10)+ddx(−2ex)=0−2ddx(ex)=−2ex.

after.problem: Given that $f(x)=2{e}^{x}-ln⁡11$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=1.$
after.worked_solution:
The derivative of ${e}^{x}$ is just ${e}^{x}$ itself. On the other hand, $-ln⁡11$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

First, using the addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x}-ln⁡11) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-ln⁡11) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})+0 \\  & =2{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(2{e}^{x})\,|}_{x=1} \\  & =2{e}^{1} \\  & =2e.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that $f(x)=2{e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=0.$
after.worked_solution:
First, using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{e}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\  & =2{e}^{x}-3(2x) \\  & =2{e}^{x}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(2{e}^{x}-6x)\,|}_{x=0} \\  & =2{e}^{0}-6\cdot 0 \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
